webTitle: Saturday Night Live: Dakota Johnson struggles through weak episode as Taylor Swift gatecrashes

fields.headline: Saturday Night Live: Dakota Johnson struggles through weak episode as Taylor Swift gatecrashes
fields.trailText: The Verity star’s awkwardness with live comedy is matched with similarly sub-par writing in an episode featuring a surprise cameo from her superstar friend
fields.bodyText: Saturday Night Live kicks off the second episode of its new season at RNC headquarters. With the midterms looking bleak for Republicans, strategists bring out some heavy hitters to record TV ads. Marco Rubio (Marcello Hernández) delivers a message in Spanish putting all of the blame on Trump (“Oh my God! He tricked us!”); a comatose Mitch McConnell (Mikey Day) is rolled in to flash the peace sign; and Vice-President JD Vance (Jeremy Culhane) tries to make his pitch for 2028, only to be laughed out of the room. Secretary of war Pete Hegseth (Colin Jost) barges in, chugging “Spider-Man’s new non-alcoholic bitch beer” to demand voters “do the gayest thing ever and vote”. Finally, president Trump (James Austin Johnson) interrupts to deliver a rambling diatribe, promising checks for five grand to voters if they re-elect Republicans (“that’s not a bribe because I have no intention to follow through on that promise”), test out some terrible new slogans (“imagination makes a Maga nation”), and record victory and concession messages, both of which are the same: “We did it, we won!” A much better cold open than last week, if still wanting. The show relied a little too heavily of Jost’s Hegseth last season, but the passage of time makes for a fun return here. Dakota Johnson hosts for the second time. The actor will celebrate her birthday at the stroke of midnight by doing the same thing she does every year: “Stand in midtown in a tight-ass latex dress looking for attention.” She devotes most of her monologue making self-deprecating jokes about her high-profile failed relationships with musicians, before her BFF Taylor Swift joins her on stage, playing reluctant therapist to the romantically-challenged star. Swift’s entrance gets a huge pop from the studio audience, but the jokes elicit little more than chuckles. Then, Johnson plays Elizabeth Banks, host of the game show Press Your Luck. Players spin a digital wheel for prizes, trying to avoid little red trouble maker The Whammy, who erases their points. Overexcited contestant Sherri (Ashley Padilla) immediately scores the million dollar prize, but stupidly continues on, only to land on the Whammy and lose it all. The same thing happens again and again, much to the chagrin of Banks and the other contestants. This is all yelling. Mean Scary Girlfriend is a cruel, icy partner who tells helpless guys the harsh truth, making their lives both easier and way, way more stressful. Not particularly funny, but a good use of Johnson’s sexy ice queen demeanor. At a hospital cafeteria, a trio of nurses spread work gossip until they’re interrupted by nerdy Eric from legal (Culhane), who uses the dish sesh to reveal sad information about himself (“I heard Eric from legal has an AI girlfriend – had, she killed herself”). The premise is promising, but it goes nowhere and quickly sputters out. This is followed by a commercial for the Glunt, the first “gun for women”. It’s a pink sidearm in the shape of a vagina, with a “hard to find” trigger and available “at the opposite of Dick’s Sporting Goods”. This one is over and done with before you even realize it. On a new Game of Thrones spin-off, Johnson and Ben Marshall play members of the royal court, whose attempts to get it on “brother-style” are continually interrupted by her fire breathing dragon, who remains in their bed chamber and likes to watch. There’s some impressive animatronics on display, but every joke falls completely flat. Indie rockers Turnstile bring some much needed energy to the show with their first set of the night, then its on to Weekend Update. Michael Che and Jost take a page from classic Late Night with Conan O’Brian’s playbook, touching on the Cornell rape case by way of Che solemnly chastising men who don’t hold predators accountable while the camera tellingly lingers on a guilty-looking Jost. The segment’s first guests are Jason and Link, the protagonists of the highly-anticipated new Grand Theft Auto and Zelda video games, respectively. The former promises “destruction, chaos, and sex”, while the latter boasts “TMPNG: too many puzzles, no guns.” Day follows up his show-stealing performance last week with another bombastic turn as the dweeby Link, getting his fellow cast members to break at just about every line. Featured player Kam Patterson pretends to be a proud “Gleek”, ecstatic over the news that Glee is coming back to TV, before Che tells him, “You don’t have to say yes to every idea the white writers pitch to you.” Then, Che welcomes on Debbie the Matchmaker (Sarah Sherman), who tries to set him up with other hopeless singles, including a phonebook’s worth of ex-felons, author and transphobe JK Rowling, a ghost, Mrs Potato Head, “the girl who crapped her pants during the Chinese marathon”, and, finally, herself. Sherman is at her bizarre best here, and its fun to see her playing off/tormenting Che instead of Jost for a change, although it feels like a missed opportunity to not include Johnson, considering she recently played a matchmaker in the popular film Materialists. At a middle school girl sleepover, three tweens watch a series of get ready with me videos on TikTok. They land on Colorado Vicky, an unwell influencer who shares insane beauty tips while getting 51/50’d and performing self-lobotomies. Just as unwell is the host girl’s dead-eyed, suicidal father (“he’s just in a funk because mom left, his boss found his Sailor Moon costume, and he just found out Draft Kings is real money”). At first, the sketch seems unfocused, but both threads are tied together satisfactorily. An episode of the TV series Amazing Tales of Truth sees a young girl (Veronika Slowikowska) attempt to bring her dying father out of a coma by singing Somewhere Over the Rainbow. It does not work. Mean and quick, this seems designed to show off Sowikowska’s impressive pipes more than anything else. And with that, the show comes to an abrupt end. Fitting, considered how rushed almost every sketch felt. Johnson is gifted a birthday cake for the curtain call, which is a nice gesture. Unfortunately, the atmosphere more resembles a wake than a party. Johnson, a talented screen actor, just does not have the chops for live comedy, and she was further hampered by the weak writing. With the exception of Day and Sherman’s turn on Update and Turnstile’s performances, this episode was a real energy vacuum.

webTitle: Medicare for All remains key pressure point for Democrats before midterms

fields.headline: Medicare for All remains key pressure point for Democrats before midterms
fields.trailText: The idea of universal health coverage in the US is embraced by party’s left but often considered a liability by centrists
fields.bodyText: Last week, 1,500 unionized nurses gathered in a large conference room at the Marriott Marquis in San Francisco to cheer for a cause they’ve championed for years: Medicare for All. Considered a radical and even fringe idea for decades, interest in sweeping healthcare reform has surged as progressive Democrats have won a series of primary victories before November’s crucial midterm elections. Most prominent among its advocates is Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate nominee from Michigan, who took the lectern before the nurses. “Medicare for who?” asked El-Sayed. “All!” the crowd shouted back. El-Sayed went on to describe why he wrote a book about Medicare for All: to answer questions about “the very simple idea that in the richest, most powerful country in the world you should not have to suffer for your healthcare”. As progressive candidates like El-Sayed prevail in primaries, and the Democratic party stresses unity in the face of its midterm challenge to Republicans, Medicare for All remains a pressure point – embraced by the party’s left but often considered a liability by centrists. “There’s too many unnecessary illnesses and unnecessary costs,” said Michelle Gutierrez Vo, president of the California Nurses Association, the National Nurses Organizing Committee and vice-president of National Nurses United – all unions that represent nurses attending the San Francisco conference. “What are we doing?” These unions have advocated for Medicare for All for years, and watched interest swell as candidates like El-Sayed picked up steam. By contrast, centrist Democrat groups, such as Third Way, consider Medicare for All an unattainable albatross. “Medicare for All has a lot of political and substantive issues,” said Gabe Horwitz, senior vice-president for the economic program at Third Way. The party is unanimous in opposition to the $1tn in healthcare cuts made by Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Democrats have taken to calling the “big, ugly bill”. The legislation is expected to result in an additional 16 million people becoming uninsured by 2034. “We want to get everyone insured, we want to lower costs and want to make care easier to use,” said Horwitz, who also said the party acknowledges that it needs to make reforms for people struggling to afford employer-sponsored health insurance. “I don’t know if there’s one Democrat in the party who wouldn’t agree with that. “There is unanimity in the goals – the ends – there’s just not necessarily unanimity in the means to get there,” said Horwitz. This divide was most recently evident in an 84-page memo sent to Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, from the cost-of-living healthcare working group. “Members of the Democratic Caucus hold a diversity of views on how to achieve universal coverage,” the memo read, “including Medicare for All” and a wide range of other more incremental policies. Centrist Democrats have sought to answer the gnawing question of what to do about soaring healthcare costs and reviled insurance company practices by proposing incremental reform – a strategy that builds off the Affordable Care Act (ACA) passed by the Obama administration. A healthcare bill of rights, more government subsidies to health insurance companies to offset costs to consumers, and some version of a “public option”, or a government-sponsored health insurance plan that people could buy into. For years, the party’s left has offered a proposition at once seen as radical by US standards and typical by many of the world’s industrialized democracies: a single-payer health system sponsored by the government. “All Democrats from 1948 on have been in favor of universal healthcare – that’s been in every democratic platform since literally Harry Truman,” said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, whose recent analysis of primary victories across the political spectrum found mainstream candidates continue to win. “That’s not the issue – the issue is how do you do it.” What’s more, said Kamarck, the issue is one likely to simmer long past the primaries. US health reform is a virtual nonstarter while Republicans hold the Oval Office. But if Democrats won a “trifecta” in 2028, “then this is going to be a really big issue”. At present, the US health system is a patchwork of different insurers, or “payers”, all of which are subsidized by US taxpayers. Four large programs dominate the mix: employer-sponsored health insurance covers almost half of Americans (48% of the population), Medicare covers people older than 65 (14.8%), Medicaid covers low-income and disabled people (20.4%) and Obamacare allows people to buy private insurance as individuals (6.6%), all according to Kaiser Family Foundation. About 27 million people (8.2%) lack insurance entirely. About one in four Americans are “underinsured”, or have high health costs relative to their incomes. Across these various programs, the US government plans to spend $33.6tn through 2034. This includes subsidies for the private insurance Americans get through their jobs, for which employers receive a tax break. That is equal to 7.4% of gross domestic product. As a point of reference, the United Kingdom spends about 11.9% of GDP to insure everyone in the country, according to the Commonwealth Fund. Total US health spending is 18% of GDP – far more than comparable countries. Although the slogan Medicare for All has a somewhat loose definition, a bill repeatedly introduced in Congress provides for a Medicare-style single-payer system, with universal health coverage. Private insurers would be barred from duplicating services. Because healthcare as an industry represents 18% of US gross domestic product (GDP), and such a dramatic transition would inevitably disrupt thousands of jobs, the bill also provides for temporary worker compensation. But for advocates of Medicare for All, such as Gutierrez Vo, anything else is, “a patch-up – it’s not a fix”. “Just like nurses take care of the whole patient– that’s like taking care of a leg and letting the rest be ill,” he said. “That’s silly.”

webTitle: Trump sets off on midterm blitz – are his trademark rallies a liability for Republicans?

fields.headline: Trump sets off on midterm blitz – are his trademark rallies a liability for Republicans?
fields.trailText: Rallies have been mainstay of president’s brand but even some in his own party fear voters are sick of the sight of him
fields.bodyText: “Get your asses in that car.” That was Donald Trump’s order, he later recalled, to his motorcade after foul weather grounded Air Force One in Texas on Thursday. The 85-mile dash to Oklahoma at nearly 100mph was proof that nothing can keep Trump from a Trump rally. Which might not be the good news for Republicans it once was. As the US president embarked on a 32-day campaign blitz aimed at helping them defend narrow congressional majorities in next month’s midterms, some fear that he is driving them towards an electoral wipeout. Trump’s approval rating is at an all-time low. Voters are angry about the cost of living, the Iran war and excessive immigration crackdowns. Some Republicans are moving to distance themselves from a man they now see as more liability than asset. Wherever he turns, the outlook is grim as he sets off on an expected schedule of five to seven rallies a week. “They’ve been a mainstay of his brand, but they’re also the engine of his doom,” Steve Schmidt, a political strategist, said of Trump’s signature campaign rallies. “Everybody knows the obvious, which is that his presence hurts every Republican candidate on the ballot because the race is fundamentally about Trump and the American people are sick and tired of him.” Schmidt added: “He’s surrounded by people who tell him that he’s beloved and that the answer to his problem is to keep talking, to keep performing, to keep doing the rallies, that the answer is more, not less. These rallies have become his lead weight, his proverbial anchor that’s going to drown them all.” Even in a hyper-digital age, Trump’s rallies have shown the enduring power of live performance. The atmosphere, somewhere between cult worship, rock concert and partisan sports event, offers his followers a sense of belonging. Since launching his bid for president in 2015 he has held roughly a thousand of them, though definitions of what counts as a full “rally” can vary. Blake Marnell, a rally regular in a brick-patterned suit resembling Trump’s border wall, was in Oklahoma on Thursday night. He said: “Getting in the motorcade, driving 100 miles an hour to Durant – he’s not gonna let stuff get in his way. He enjoys the rallies. They’re energising for the crowd and for him. It’s a way for him to connect with the grassroots.” Once in Durant, Trump again basked in the adulation of the rally crowd. Having spotted two diehard supporters being interviewed by TV crews outside the venue, he replayed the clip and summoned them on to the main stage. “You can’t miss big, strong, handsome Oklahoma studs,” he said. “Where are you? Come up here!” The pair were white, male and elderly. One, wearing a green Trump cap and grey Trump T-shirt, stepped up to the microphone and said: “Thank you, President Trump, for all you do. Every day you work harder than any American I know.” The other, wearing a red Make America Great Again cap and red T-shirt, said: “Absolute honour of a lifetime to be with the greatest president this country has ever had!” Marnell, from San Diego, California, loved this example of Trump showmanship and dismissed the notion that his rallies are hurting rather than helping Republicans. “That’s ridiculous. How many years now have we heard critics saying that Trump is done, the end is near, the walls are closing in, this is the beginning of the end, he can’t possibly win. “They’ve written him off so many times, I don’t know why people listen when they say things like that. It makes no sense to me. This election is, to an extent larger than normal, going to be swayed by turnout and so turnout is the goal of these rallies.” Yet beneath the carnival atmosphere in Oklahoma lay an undercurrent of anxiety and a new vulnerability. At one point Trump entreated the audience, “Pretend I’m running, please,” and begged them to contact friends and relatives. He openly admitted the Republican party’s precarious footing across the national map. “We’re worried about Michigan, we’re worried about Texas, we’re worried about a few states.” He has cause to be worried. A recent survey by the Associated Press-Norc Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of US adults approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy – a new low. Only about three in 10 approve of how he is handling his job as president. In a striking sign of trouble, a major Republican political action committee has reportedly pulled back its spending in North Carolina, the only battleground state Trump won in all three of his presidential bids, diverting its resources instead to ruby red Kansas. Even among dedicated fans who have followed him around the country and become known as “front-row Joes” at his rallies, doubts are creeping in. Trisha Hope, a “front-row Joe” who once bought an RV and published a book of Trump’s tweets to fund her travel, recently declared him a “fraud and liar”. Speaking to Politico, Hope cited Trump’s abrupt dismissal of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation during a cabinet meeting, as well as his unfulfilled promises regarding the war in Iran. “If we do lose the midterms and he is impeached again, I will be walking the halls of Congress in support of that impeachment,” she said. But when confronted with the negative numbers, the president has sounded like a man in denial, preferring to discuss his architectural projects in Washington including a new White House ballroom. At his stop in Denton, north-west of Dallas, Texas, earlier on Thursday, he insisted that inflation was entirely the fault of Joe Biden as he dismissed concerns about everyday living costs. “We have the greatest numbers of any president in the history of our country, and I can’t get the word out,” Trump lamented to workers at a truck factory. “Maybe we’re doing a bad job selling it.” John Zogby, an author and pollster, said: “It looks as if he’s very out of touch with the reality of most Americans. Of course, he has spent a lifetime being out of touch and creating that kind of lifestyle for himself.” The 80-year-old’s rally performances have noticeably deteriorated, Zogby argues, marked by rambling digressions that fail to speak to the immediate anxieties of ordinary voters. “Number one, he is tending to digress. He’s not on his best form. But secondly, when he does address affordability, it’s, ‘Wait and see, just a little longer, the war will be over.’ It’s not connecting.” The strain between Trump and Republicans was highlighted this week by a secret audio recording from a high-dollar fundraiser. On the tape, obtained by the New York Times, the Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton – whose Senate campaign has been floundering under the weight of scandals – was overheard candidly admitting to donors that Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas damaged Republican prospects. Paxton admitted: “When we did that convention, it dropped our numbers; everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now? Yeah. It’s not good. I wish there was something we could do to turn that around, but obviously nothing.” At the event in Denton, Trump praised Paxton as one of his “most loyal people”, while jokingly adding: “I have to always remember that because he can be a pain in the ass sometimes, I’ll be honest. Is he here, by the way? Oh, there he is – good. I didn’t even know if he’s here. I don’t care!” The president also insisted: “My heart is in it like never before.” Yet his early campaign schedule has raised eyebrows. He is spending the first five days of October in Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska, all reliable Republican strongholds in recent years. Critics say it shows that he is on the defensive. Schmidt, who worked for Republicans George W Bush and John McCain, observed: “The BS stops on the map. When you’re campaigning in October as a Republican in those states, not only does it mean you’re losing, it means you’re losing in a biblical sense, an end-times sense. The reality is that there’s no safe Republican anywhere in the country. That’s why he’s there.” Generic congressional polls show Democrats holding a lead approaching double digits, raising the spectre of a “blue wave” that could sweep away Republican majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. A Republican official said: “We’re not going to send Potus to areas where it would be hurtful to our candidates.” For Democrats, Trump’s tour through safe conservative territory is an open admission of weakness. Michelle Lujan Grisham, the governor of New Mexico, suggested that reminding voters of Trump’s presidency in the final weeks of the campaign is a strategic blunder on his part. “In those places, I would hope that it hurts,” she said. “People are angry and you shouldn’t be reminding them. So, I’m going to say go ahead. Maybe he should spend some more time in Texas.” Lujan Grisham criticised Trump’s second term, pointing to what she described as a litany of broken promises, economic mismanagement and foreign policy overreach. “He promised to deliver for Americans and he did none of the above. He’s in a war that nobody wants in Iran that he can’t get out of. He’s doing nothing for inflation; he’s making it worse. And he certainly isn’t addressing affordability.” She singled out the administration’s aggressive policies under Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which she described as a major moral and political liability for the White House. “ICE of course is a huge liability for the White House and this administration, just given they continue to detain both lawfully present individuals and Americans. We’ve had Americans lose their lives, and we’ve devastated whole communities and families. He’s in real trouble.” Trump hopes the campaign rallies that featured so prominently in his victories in 2016 and 2024 will do the trick again on behalf of Republicans in 2026. They will also feed his appetite for the cheering faithful that have become central to his political identity. Schmidt sees a parallel with the faded Hollywood star from one of Trump’s favourite films, Sunset Boulevard. “He needs attention like Norma Desmond and that’s who he’s become here at the nadir of his presidency as he moves from king of the hill into decrepit lame duck. All of the Führer rallies in the red states don’t change the fact. There’s no amount of money that could be spent on his behalf, no amount of rallies, nothing that can save him from the judgment that’s coming down on his head.”

webTitle: Republicans say they hate communists. So why do they like Donald Trump?

fields.headline: Republicans say they hate communists. So why do they like Donald Trump?
fields.trailText: Trump supporters may be surprised to learn the state takeover of means of production is not driven by the left
fields.bodyText: Americans will never accept the Democratic party’s slide to the left, or so desperate Republicans are hoping. With the midterm elections fast upon us, Zohran Mamdani’s promise of a few city-run bodegas in New York City will scare the bejeezus out of middle America. Disgust over the democratic socialists’ unicorn-and-puppy promises of a world without capitalism will keep the Republicans in power. Leading the charge against the new reds-under-the-bed is Donald Trump. “Together, we will defeat communism,” Trump promised in his recent TV ads. Trump’s supporters might be surprised to discover that the United States is, indeed, sliding in the direction of a command and control economy. But the state takeover of the means of production is not being driven by the left. The grab for the US’s productive resources is the project of none other than Trump – who, it’s a fair guess, has never read Lenin. The latest evidence comes in data crunched by the V-Dem project in Sweden, which measures the erosion of democracy around the world. It built a scale to gauge “state ownership of the economy”. As noted by Cullen Hendrix from the Peterson Institute for International Economics, from 2002 to 2024, the US ranked among the four countries with the least state control. In 2025, the first year of Trump’s second term, it dropped from second place to 16th. By November of last year, the Trump administration had spent more than $10bn taking stakes in companies he deemed essential for national security, from Intel to a range of ventures mining for critical minerals. It also acquired an option to take a stake in Westinghouse, which makes nuclear reactors. And it blackmailed Nippon Steel into granting Trump’s Washington a “golden share” in exchange for the go-ahead to purchase US Steel. To be fair, Trump’s acquisitiveness notwithstanding, the US is not even close to flirting with the flavor of socialism favored by the Soviet Union and its satellites in the second half of the 20th century. By the V-Dem accounting, Washington’s stake in the economy is still smaller than in 163 countries. Government-run companies are a standard feature in many market economies. The Norwegian government has a majority stake in its massive oil company, which puts the country in 18th place. Even “communist” countries are pretty capitalist: private companies contribute 60% of China’s GDP. And in a geopolitical landscape shaped by competition with China, there is a reasonable case to be made for Washington to take equity stakes in industries that are critical for American leadership and security, and which might not develop autonomously in competition with rivals heavily subsidized by Beijing. Yet Trump’s wanton lunge for private assets lacks the discipline required for this kind of strategic positioning. The president’s statist leanings mark a dramatic break with the market-focused presidencies of his recent predecessors, Democrat and Republican. The question is, what motivates him? His appetites are embedded in a body of thought that is skeptical, if not outright hostile, towards essential building blocks of the global market economy. He has pushed back against globalization since his first term in office, seemingly drawn to the Marxist-inspired dependency theory, which washed across Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s proposing protectionism and state industrial policy as a path to economic development. His lust to control the economy is there for all to see. Though the supreme court already slapped down his attempt to take over trade policy from Congress, he is still threatening to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT”. His promise to give $5,000 to every American if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November’s elections underscores how he views the state’s coffers as his private piggy bank. Even his commie-bashing ads were paid for by taxpayer dollars. Still, he clearly has no interest in the dictatorship of the proletariat, caring little if at all for the fate of the downtrodden. His preferred flavor of redistribution takes from those on the bottom to give to those on the top. If anything, Trump reminds us that socialism is not the only ideological justification for state projects to take control over resources and wealth. Watching the US president bow to Xi Jinping last week, it’s tempting to think that Trump wants to emulate China’s leader. Xi gets to rule unimpeded over more than one billion Chinese. He gets to shape China’s society and economy at will – purging this rival, raising that sycophant to power. But Xi’s China is too disciplined for Trump. The Chinese leader still relies on hordes of technocrats to execute a coherent strategy aimed to achieve technological superiority. The US president doesn’t have the attention span for this kind of thing. Rather, Trump’s model might be Vladimir Putin, who rules Russia like a fiefdom. Or maybe one of those dictators the US used to support in Latin America during the cold war: Haiti’s Papa Doc Duvalier or Anastasio Somoza in Nicaragua, who saw government as a tool to enrich their families and cement dynasties in power. If nothing else, Trump’s dealings with crypto suggest he views his administration as a road to family riches. Karl Marx may not be Trump’s guiding light. But his writings can help understand Trump’s place in history. Marx proposes that his tome The 18th Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, about the 1851 coup that brought Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte to power in France, was meant to “demonstrate how the class struggle in France created circumstances and relationships that made it possible for a grotesque mediocrity to play a hero’s part”. Americans may be grateful that their most recent class struggles didn’t produce a homegrown Lenin. But they did deliver Donald Trump. Perhaps this does not condemn the US to an autocratic future. Hendrix points out that while Trump “clearly wants to be king”, the US’s political economy may not let him. Putin managed to establish autocratic rule over a fairly primitive, oil-based economy. This kind of control “is much harder to achieve in a modern complex economy” such as that of the United States, Hendrix noted. You can’t simply seize the oil to run the place. Though Trump may fail, Americans’ acquiescence as he grabs for power raises a question for those who freak out over Mamdani’s city-run bodegas: why is Trump’s lurch to take over the American economy any better than what they hear from the Democratic Socialists of America? Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

webTitle: Trump wants control of South America. If Bolsonaro Jr wins in Brazil, that could become a reality | Steve Bloomfield

fields.headline: Trump wants control of South America. If Bolsonaro Jr wins in Brazil, that could become a reality
fields.trailText: The US president has taken credit for far-right victories across Latin America, but those wins have had more to do with fears of gang crime than his meddling, says journalist Steve Bloomfield
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump has enjoyed very few foreign policy victories since returning to power. From failed wars to failed peace processes, his second term in office has been marked by one costly blunder on the world stage after another. In Latin America, though, the US president has a different story to tell. His administration’s national security strategy outlined how the US wanted to “restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere”. It was a brazen document, laying out how his government would interfere in the political life of countries it considered part of its sphere of influence, rewarding governments and movements that are “broadly aligned with our principles and strategy”. To this end, Trump bailed out Argentina to the tune of $40bn and threatened to withdraw the funding if President Javier Milei’s party lost the midterm elections. In Colombia, he repeatedly bullied and threatened the leftwing president, Gustavo Petro, hitting him with personal sanctions and accusing him of being an “illegal drug leader”. And most dramatically, he invaded Venezuela and kidnapped its president. The day after Nicolás Maduro was brought to the US, the state department posted a picture of Trump above the slogan “This is OUR hemisphere”. Over the past 18 months, seven rightwing or far-right candidates have won presidential elections across Latin America. In most of them, Trump openly backed the winning candidate. “We’re doing very well in South America,” Trump said last month. “Lots of people that I got elected.” This weekend, he will be hoping to add the greatest prize of all: Brazil, South America’s biggest country and its largest economy. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, is neck and neck with the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. If he wins, Trump wins – and the hemisphere really will be his. The White House has not simply been watching the election from afar. Since Trump returned to power in January 2025, administration officials and Maga-world allies have been doing what they can to damage Lula and boost the Bolsonaros. Initially, the aim of the support was to keep Jair Bolsonaro out of jail. Like Trump, he had not accepted defeat at the ballot box when he lost in the 2022 general election. Like Trump, his supporters stormed government buildings. But there were two crucial differences in Brazil – the seriousness of Bolsonaro’s attempt to hold on to power, and the determination of Brazilians that he should be held to account. Investigators uncovered a sprawling conspiracy led by Bolsonaro and seven of his closest allies to keep him in power. It included an astonishing plot to kill Lula and his running mate, as well as a supreme court judge. A draft decree had been written that would overturn the result. The military would step in and ensure Bolosnaro returned to power. But the plot failed and Bolsonaro and allies, including his defence minister and the navy chief, were arrested and put on trial. In response, Trump threatened in July 2025 to impose a 50% tariff on all imports from Brazil, arguing the case against Bolsonaro was a “witch hunt”. This blatant attempt at interfering in the judicial procedure of another country backfired. Lula made clear he wouldn’t bow to US pressure, the trial went ahead and Bolsonaro was found guilty and sentenced to 27 years in prison. Lula also received a bump in the polls after standing up to Trump. In July, as the election campaign was kicking into gear, Trump tried his tariff trick again, imposing a new 25% rate on some Brazilian goods. The state department then tried to dispatch two officials to Brazil to investigate “electoral integrity” – Brazil denied them visas, accusing the officials of coming to “meddle in Brazil’s elections”. In the final weeks of the campaign, Lula has leaned into those accusations. A recent advert accused Flávio Bolsonaro of being “Trump’s candidate” and said the US president wants “to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust”. What remains unclear is whether the White House’s strategy in Brazil is working. “Some in Brazil joke that Lula’s most effective surrogate is Trump,” Brian Winter, editor in chief of Americas Quarterly, told me. Indeed, while Latin American countries have undoubtedly moved to the right in the past 18 months, US interference, despite Trump’s boasts, has arguably had little direct impact. In Peru and Chile, the Trump-aligned candidates were careful not to seek his endorsement for fear it would cause more trouble than it was worth. In Bolivia, the leftwing Mas government was responsible for its own downfall, winning just 3.16% in last year’s election after 20 years of increasingly chaotic rule. The biggest reason countries have moved to the right has nothing to do with the US and everything to do with safety and security at home. Organised crime gangs, many of them linked to drug trafficking, are increasing in power. As Crisis Group put it in a report last year, while drug-related organised crime has been a problem across the continent for decades, “never has it spread so wide, and rarely has it penetrated so deeply into states and communities”. The failure of leftwing governments to deal with the problem has hurt them more than Trump’s attempts at interference. If there is a foreign president whose policies are having an influence on Latin America, it’s El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. His authoritarian clampdown, which has involved arresting tens of thousands of people, mostly without legal process, has become a model for other rightwing leaders in countries beset by gang and drug cartel-related violence. Democracy has been eroded and human rights trampled upon, but Bukele claims that his strategy – best described as “security populism” – has turned one of the most violent countries in the world into one of the safest. Other rightwing populists have found success in vowing to emulate him. In Brazil, Flávio Bolsonaro has made a crackdown on drug cartels and organised crime gangs the centrepiece of his campaign. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people,” he said at a recent campaign stop, vowing to chemically castrate rapists and reduce the age of criminal responsibility. On this issue, Trump may have an influence. The US decision in May to designate two criminal organisations – the Red Command and First Capital Command (PCC) – as terrorist organisations has put Lula on the back foot. Bolsonaro has campaigned relentlessly on the issue, accusing Lula of weakness. Lula has talked about targeting the crime boss “who lives in a penthouse”, but has been more comfortable campaigning on improvements he wants to make in education and health. Bolsonaro Jr, should he win, will almost certainly sign Brazil up to Trump’s Shield of the Americas, a coalition of 18 rightwing Latin American and Caribbean heads of state that promises to use “lethal military force to destroy the sinister cartels and terrorist networks”. Trump arguably paved the way for this new generation of Latin American political leader. His first victory in 2016 showed that posing as an outsider, using coarse language and embracing authoritarianism could be popular. Jair Bolsonaro was the first to emulate him, embracing the “Trump of the Tropics” tag. If Flávio Bolsonaro wins this month – either on Sunday or in the probable second round on 25 October – Trump’s ideology will dominate the continent. It is likely to outlast the man himself. The rise of organised crime has spread fear across the continent and, at the moment, the security populists are the only ones who voters believe have the answer. As long as that remains, the right’s grip on Latin America will only get stronger, regardless of who is in the White House. Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

webTitle: MS Now connects ‘blue dots’ at Texas fan event: ‘I always feel hope when I watch them’

fields.headline: MS Now connects ‘blue dots’ at Texas fan event: ‘I always feel hope when I watch them’
fields.trailText: Network at receiving end of White House press ban recently chose red state to host fan event as part of broader outreach
fields.bodyText: In 2024, Donald Trump and JD Vance carried Tarrant county, Texas, by 42,125 votes. So why, on the afternoon of 26 September, was the arena at the University of Texas-Arlington filled with nearly 5,000 super fans cheering for liberal media darlings Rachel Maddow and Lawrence O’Donnell like they were rock stars? After two years of hosting the network’s annual fan event in dark blue New York City, MS Now (formerly MSNBC) got wind that something was happening in Texas. The state, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in 37 years, might do so next month, when 37-year-old James Talarico, Texas state representative, goes up against the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, a well-known but controversial figure who ousted incumbent John Cornyn in the party’s primary with Donald Trump’s backing. “We wanted to be bigger and bolder. We wanted to go to a story that really matters (and this is one of the most important stories of the season), and we wanted to keep growing our live events business,” Marcus Mabry, senior vice-president of content strategy for MS Now, said in an interview. And, he noted, “everything is bigger in Texas”. While MS Now has a relative monopoly on older liberal Americans who still watch linear television, the network sees potential outside of its traditional coastal strongholds – much like the national Democratic party. Several MS Now hosts hinted at that growth opportunity in their onstage remarks throughout the day’s programming. “I will say, in the state of Texas, you might have a lot of neighbors that don’t vote like you, but it doesn’t mean they can’t tomorrow,” Stephanie Ruhle, an MS Now host, told the crowd. “I met so many people today whose eyes were filled with tears, and they said: ‘I’m the sole blue dot in Texas.’ How great that you are outstanding. How great that you are a special voice.” Or, as Mabry put it: “I think right now the opportunity for any journalism in the country is to stop speaking red and blue, and to start speaking to people as individuals.” In a holding room before his onstage interview with Stacey Abrams, a former Georgia state representative, Chris Hayes, an MS Now host, said viewers seem to be more “locked into the news” lately after a period of post-election malaise (and softer television ratings) in late 2024 and early 2025, particularly now that Democrats face good odds in next month’s midterm elections. “There are thousands and thousands of people here – in the middle of Texas,” he said of the event. Comparing the vibes with the months after Trump took office, “it feels like another world … We’ve had the most intense stress test in the American constitutional republic in my lifetime, and I don’t think anything is determined yet, but it certainly feels better than a year and a half ago.” The network is feeling that surge of interest. So far this year, MS Now’s primetime lineup is averaging 1.3 million viewers, up 11% from 2025. The network has seen an even bigger increase among viewers aged 25 to 54, the demographic most prized by advertisers. The event – Together In Texas: We the People 2026 – also served as something of an in-person illustration of the network’s first major direct-to-consumer offering, a membership plan – for $7.99 per month or $79.99 annually – that gives subscribers access to two daily Q&As with top hosts and reporters, a moderated discussion community for members, exclusive content, a curated daily briefing and even a collection of guided meditations. (Those in the Founders tier of the membership program had access to a special lounge at the event space.) “We’re still telling the audience what they need to know, but we’re also asking them, ‘What do you want to know, and how can we actually have a relationship where we actually are more than just delivering news to you as the voice of God,’ which fewer and fewer audience actually wants,” Mabry said. “I hope our business is learning that, because that’s the only way we survive. And we have to survive – it’s important for democracy.” With MS Now leaning into direct-to-customer products, fan service was the name of the game at the event. At one point, Rebecca Kutler, the network president, happily agreed to photograph several attenders who wanted to take photos with Laura Barrón-López, the MS Now White House correspondent, after a panel on the network’s expulsion from the building – seemingly without realizing who their amateur photographer was. “I’ll do any job!” Kutler told the Guardian. Ruhle served as the event’s unofficial “cheerleader”, as one attender said, hyping up the crowd and taking photos with fans. “Those are the people that we work for,” she said in an interview. “When you talk about the media being disconnected from the people, we are no longer – or we shouldn’t be – in the presentation business. No longer should we be sitting in newsrooms deciding here’s what we’re going to make or here’s how it has to look.” “This isn’t a political rally,” Ruhle said of the event. “This is what America is … These people make our shows better. Why wouldn’t you want to be with them?” Ahead of the event, several attenders said it was a no-brainer for MS Now to host the event in Texas – and said they were committed to watching the network as a purveyor of both reliable information and a much-needed sense of optimism. Ronnie Thomas, a 47-year-old Dallas resident who works in automotive sales, said he was “very happy” to be able to see Maddow and his other favorite hosts with only a short drive. “I like getting more of the truth,” his wife Rachael, also 47, said. “And it feels like they are closer to what the true state of things are compared to some of the things we see on other stations.” Former Republican Leslie Lesher, 73, and her spouse Joni Dennis, 68, said they watch MS Now “almost all day” every day. “These are our favorite people,” Lesher said. “I know they have knowledge that we don’t have. I always feel hope when I watch them.” Ruhle shared her sentiments. “A lot of people are scared about the state of the world,” she said. “They’re scared of the state of democracy. And I just think we’re all in this together.”

webTitle: The Tejano singer trying to win back Latinos who voted for Trump, one quinceañera at a time

fields.headline: The Tejano singer trying to win back Latinos who voted for Trump, one quinceañera at a time
fields.trailText: Bobby Pulido has a strategy: show up at the 15th birthday parties that are a rite of passage in the Texas borderlands – and flip a key House district for Democrats
fields.bodyText: It took all of two minutes for Bobby Pulido’s electoral stealth weapon to come into play. The Tejano music star turned Democratic congressional candidate had barely begun canvassing in the high school football stadium in Edinburg, Texas, when a 15-year-old girl came rushing up to him. “Señor Pulido! Señor Pulido!” she cried. A few months ago, she told him, he had made a surprise appearance at her quinceañera, the coming-of-age girls’ 15th birthday party that is a rite of passage in these US borderlands. He had serenaded her with Desvelado, his blockbuster love song, which though released three decades ago retains a treasured place in Tejano – that is Hispanic Texan – culture. The brief encounter gave a glimpse into one of the key dynamics of Pulido’s bid to flip Texas’s 15th congressional district. He calls it the “quinceañera strategy”. The tactic was handed to him, inadvertently, by his rival, the two-term incumbent Republican congresswoman Monica De La Cruz. In March, she posted a video deriding her opponent as a lowly quinceañera singer. The election, she said, “isn’t about who you want performing at your niece’s quinceañera. It’s about who you trust with your family’s future.” Pulido pounced. He counter-posted his own video in which he accused De La Cruz of belittling a cherished local tradition and encouraged families in the district planning a quinceañera to invite him. “I’d be honored to stop by and celebrate with you,” he said. Within 24 hours, Pulido’s campaign had been inundated with over 1,000 invitations. By the time the Guardian went canvassing with him in September, that number had surpassed 5,000. He has now performed at 81 quinceañeras and counting. Each one is attended by scores of family and friends, most of whom are eligible voters and many of whom livestream the event on their smartphones, broadcasting it to additional scores of eligible voters. “She presented us with an opportunity for a very unique kind of field plan,” Abel Prado, Pulido’s campaign manager, said. The ‘quinceañera strategy’ Pulido, 53, is hoping to convert the quinceañera strategy and the rest of the tireless retail politics that he is doing into a winning political formula. His mission: to take back the congressional seat, and in the process both help the national Democratic party regain control of the US House and teach it a lesson or two about Mexican American politics. Much is riding on his success. It’s not just that flipping Texas 15 could give Democrats the edge they need to take back control of the House of Representatives. The stakes are also huge for the Rio Grande valley itself, the overwhelmingly Hispanic border region in south Texas that for over a century was solidly Democratic but swung hard for Donald Trump in 2024. Trump won the district, which is 81% Mexican American and which runs for over 300 miles from the border to San Antonio, by 18 points. How Pulido fares in the November midterm elections could have ripple effects for fellow Democrat James Talarico’s currently neck-and-neck fight for a US Senate seat against the state’s scandal-ridden Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton. Talarico’s chance of success is also heavily dependent on Latino turnout. And in the widest sense, Pulido’s message has bearings on the national Democratic party as it debates how to counter the dramatic inroads made by Trump two years ago when he smashed records and garnered 55% of Texas’s Hispanic vote. Pulido made sure to display his Tejano stripes as he strutted around the Edinburg stadium, while cheerleaders and a marching band filled the night air with colour and noise. Dressed in jeans and denim shirt, cowboy boots and hat, he moved confidently through the crowd of high-school football fans. He shook the hand of everyone he met, chatting to supporters on both sides of the bleachers – a calculated move as both high school teams, Sabrecats and Yellowjackets, are in the 15th district. (The Sabrecats won 31-14.) And yet almost everyone in attendance was too young to vote – so what was the point? “To win re-election,” Pulido quipped, without missing a beat. Then, with more reflection, he added: “If you treat kids good, their parents will like you.” Pulido has a catchphrase: “Any occasion, big or small.” He means it. The football game was the 526th campaign event he had attended in person. His record is 12 such stops in a single day. When Pulido sat down to talk with the Guardian, he emphasised accessibility was a critical element of his campaign. It’s his answer, he said, to the increasingly polarised left-right media bubbles that keep voters divided. “The only way I can break through is to actually get in front of people the old-fashioned way. Then people can hear me. They can look me in the eye, and decide for themselves whether I’m full of shit or not.” Direct connection with voters also allows Pulido, who has roots stretching back seven generations in the Rio Grande valley, to play his ace card: his near-universal name recognition in the region. Desvelado (“sleepless”) was his first, and is still his biggest, hit – the 1995 album of the same name went platinum, and the song has been played 615m times on Spotify. He has won two Latin Grammys for best Tejano album; the day before we met he celebrated yet another nomination for the award, for Una Tuya, Una Mía, Vol 2. If the massive popularity of Desvelado gives him an entree with younger and middle-aged Tejanos, he can count on his father to grab the attention of older voters. José Roberto Pulido, 75, is a Tejano music star in his own right, having enjoyed a large local following in the 1970s and 80s. In Pulido’s analysis, Trump lured so many of these Tejano voters away from the Democratic party in 2024 because he spoke to their longing for the American dream. There’s a popular phrase in the valley: “We know we’re broke, but don’t tell us we’re poor.” Pulido said: “If you’re poor, you’ve already lost; if you’re broke, you could still make it one day. Trump kind of won because of that message. ‘Look at me, I’m rich, and some of my richness will transfer to you’ – that was music to people’s ears.” Trump’s promise to close the US-Mexico border also spoke to many people in the valley. The disruption caused by record numbers of undocumented immigrants crossing into the US during the Biden administration was especially felt in this frontier zone, and many Tejano US citizens bridled against it despite their own immigrant heritage. “Under Biden, the border was chaotic,” Pulido said. “The tent cities, the visible hardship, so many coming across.” Since the return of Trump to the White House, however, Pulido believes that the president has squandered much of that goodwill. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made Texas the ground zero of its mass deportation efforts, notably so given the central position the state commands within Trump’s Maga universe. Figures compiled by the Deportation Data Project show that ICE made 12,086 arrests in July in Texas. That was almost twice the number in the next most intensely targeted states, Florida (7,405) and California (6,464). Pulido is convinced that Trump will pay a price in November for this blanket assault on Texas immigrants. “People are angry, ICE enforcement is splitting up families and spreading fear. And it’s hurting our economy. There’s not a building in the Rio Grande valley that was put up without immigrant hands. None.” He added: “There is a reckoning coming, that’s for sure. I see it. We’ve polled it. People don’t like what the Republican party is doing.” The most recent survey of the 15th district, from Texas Southern University, puts Pulido five points ahead of De La Cruz (50% to 45%). Among Latino likely voters, the gap widens to 25 points (60% to 35%). “This election is showing that the Trump bubble is burst,” the co-author of the opinion poll, Mark Jones, professor of political science at Rice University, said. “We did see a temporary shift towards Trump among Latino voters, but now we’re coming back to a more standard status quo.” The Guardian spoke to several 15th district voters who two years ago enthusiastically cast their ballots for Trump yet who have grown disaffected and disillusioned. Yajaira Martinez, 43, is a naturalized citizen who came to the US from Mexico when she was six. In 2024, she voted for Trump because she believed his promises about bringing down prices and improving the economy, and because she supported his desire for a stronger border. She heard him pledge to remove undocumented immigrants with criminal records. “If you want to take the criminals out of the country, by all means go ahead,” she said. But she did not expect the ICE dragnet of hardworking people trying to make a go for their families. She knows several people who have been deported even though they had legitimate work permits. “ICE is breaking the law, they are assaulting, they are chasing down. They are terrorising. This administration doesn’t care about anybody’s rights.” Juan Cantu, 66, was born in Mexico but lives in the US, and as a naturalized citizen is entitled to vote. He makes an income both as a cabinet maker and rancher. He voted for Trump in 2024 because he was fed up with Democrats talking about social issues such as abortion and trans people using women’s bathrooms, and he thought Trump would be on his side as un trabajador, a worker. But he’s been appalled as he watches “the politics of Trump spinning out of control, harming so many working people”. The Iran war, which he said he does not understand, and tariffs have pushed the diesel that powers his tractor to $6 a gallon, and that’s a problem. As for Pulido, Cantu likes his father’s Tejano music. “That’s the music of my época,” he said. And he warms to the candidate’s politics. “From what I’ve heard, he wants to help the poor, the working people.” He will vote for Pulido. Juan Pablo Lopez, 41, a first-generation Mexican American born in the US, is the owner of a real estate and construction company in McAllen. He voted for Trump because he liked the way he spoke the language of business. In the past year, though, it’s turned sour for Lopez. He estimates that about 60 of his co-workers and friends have disappeared, rounded up by ICE and detained then deported. He said he had come to conclusion that Trump is not the friend of Tejanos. “Everybody here believed in him, and instead of helping us, he’s hurting us.” As for his vote in November, it’s complicated. Lopez said he likes Pulido. “I was born and raised with his music. He’s a family guy, and I like that he’s very conservative.” What he doesn’t like is that Pulido is running as a Democrat, a party he thinks has a “Robin Hood mentality”. “They take from the rich to give to the poor – let’s give everybody food stamps, let’s make sure everybody’s on housing. I’m a hardworking American.” That leaves him in a bind. “I’m faced with a very hard decision of who I’m going to vote for. I don’t want to vote Democrat, but look at what Trump has done to us.” It’s Pulido’s challenge to overcome the hesitation of voters like Lopez. He must harness their patent anger towards Trump’s handling of immigration and the economy, and persuade them that not all Democrats are leftist progressives. As he faces this challenge, Pulido is careful to emphasise his conservative convictions while avoiding talking in party political terms. The race is not about Democrat versus Republican, but about Bobby versus Monica. “I do not mention blue waves. Not ever.” There is a populist side to Pulido’s politics that bears comparison to Bernie Sanders. He denounces “crony capitalism” and demands that corporate money is removed from US elections. Pulido doesn’t have health insurance because “it’s not worth it”. “I should not feel obligated to feed those monsters. Health insurance companies get away with it, and doctors can’t even be doctors any more,” he said. Beneath the populist patina, his innate cultural conservatism – typical of this border region – is glaringly apparent. He is a man of faith, and is personally opposed to abortion though his policy is that he would not impose his views on anybody else: “Pro-life is a choice too. It’s my choice,” he said. He opposes restrictions on oil and gas extraction, including fracking, as they account for a significant proportion of the valley’s jobs. He wants the border to remain locked down even after Trump has gone, though he wants that to be done humanely. There’s no doubting his support for the second amendment. He named his son Remington, after the Remington 700 bolt-action rifle that he loves. If you described a politician with that set of convictions to a person in Brooklyn or Santa Monica they might assume he were a moderate Republican. So what makes him a Democrat? “I’m a Democrat because I lead with my democratic heart,” he said. “I understand that there are people out there who need help, and that it’s my obligation as a Catholic and as a Christian to do what I can to help my fellow neighbor.” In all this, there is an implicit criticism of the national leadership of the Democratic party and what he regards as its coastal elite prejudices. “In music, you have to know your audience. I’m smart enough to know that you don’t take a symphonic orchestra to the dancehall – people want to dance. But that’s what my party is doing, taking the east coast and west coast politics of the liberal elites and bringing them to where they do not resonate.” Warming to the theme, he said: “What plays well in New York City likely won’t play well among Democratic voters in the valley. The party has become too one-size-fits-all, and that’s a big mistake.” His main takeaway from his months running for congressional office is that Democrats “let other people define us”. “When I first told people in this district that I was running as a Democrat, their automatic assumption was that I was going to take away their guns, that I was for trans in women’s sports, that I was going to take away their oil and gas jobs,” he said. “That’s the narrative they were fed by Republicans.” As the 3 November election gets closer, and the temperature of the race rises, De La Cruz has tried to stall Pulido’s advance by hitting him with negative attack ads casting him as a “corrupt liberal celebrity”. In particular, she has focused on revelations that an accordionist in Pulido’s band who played on the recording of Desvelado later became a registered sex offender. De La Cruz has accused Pulido of “endangering our families”. He counters that he only discovered his band member’s sex crimes record years later. The Republican has also charged Pulido with demeaning voters, basing the claim on a 2020 video that has resurfaced in which he is seen laughing as a comedy host made remarks about women’s bodies following childbirth and on past social media posts in which he used racist and homophobic slurs. Pulido has admitted that some of his comments crossed the line and apologised for them. But he argues that De La Cruz has supported a president who has repeatedly attacked women’s appearances. So far there is insufficient data from opinion polls to know whether the mud is sticking. Republican efforts to win congressional seats in south Texas through redistricting may also backfire on De La Cruz. The 15th district was redrawn with the aim of preserving her lead while at the same time attempting to flip neighboring seats from the Democrats. As a result almost two-thirds of the voters in the reconfigured 15th district are new to De La Cruz, with many voters having little or no idea who she is. That matters when she is up against someone with almost universal name recognition like Pulido. “When I saw the map, I was very happy,” he said with a grin. Asked to comment on Pulido’s political record and the state of the race, De La Cruz’s campaign manager, James Shook, described Pulido as “a silver-spooned scumbag who enabled a sex predator”. “Anyone starstruck by this pedo-protecting loser should be ashamed of themselves,” he said in the statement. There is a bittersweetness to the looming election for Pulido. He is potentially poised to pull off a historic victory that would send him to Washington where a whole new political life would await him. But it would mark the end of his other life as a Tejano musician. Last year he embarked on a farewell tour, and just before we met his final performance was announced. It will take place in Edinburg, 17 days before the election. He’s calling it La Última Desvelada.
